A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research despite the title change. All 18 pages of v3 and 20 pages of v4, including appendices, are readable; retained experiments, equations, and figures can be matched reliably.

before.justification: V3 reports original experiments on synthetic counting and addition, plus continued-pretraining experiments evaluated on MMLU and CommonsenseQA.

after.justification: V4 retains these original experiments and reports additional MMLU loss distributions and a training-loss analysis.

M1.justification: The synthetic Transformer architecture, distributional framework, and Qwen procedure remain unchanged. Both versions reinitialize the final attention layer and LM head before full-parameter continued pretraining. The revised explanation of maximum-token loss does not change its existing formula.

E1.justification: Both versions use counting, reverse-order addition with index hints, MMLU, CommonsenseQA, and C4 news. Added loss analyses and revised mixture proportions remain within these existing tasks and data domains.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain the same Qwen2.5 model sizes, base-model reference scores, and random-guess baselines. No evaluated comparison method is added or removed.

E3.justification: V4 adds MMLU NLL evaluation and a final-training-loss control. The appendix Qwen2.5-1.5B mixture grid changes from 0.01–5% MMLU to selected ratios within 0.02–0.10% (v3 Figure 15 versus v4 Figure 17). Existing architectures, epoch budgets, learning rates, and synthetic evaluation lengths remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 3.4 substantially extends the investigation of alternative explanations to LMs: Figures 8 and 17 examine continuous-loss multimodality, while Figure 9 tests whether similar clustering occurs in training loss. V3 examined continuous metrics only on synthetic tasks. These additions directly test the validity of the natural-language extension.

E5.justification: The reported population for the main MMLU experiments increases from 20 to 80 reinitializations per setting. V4 Appendix E.1 explicitly retains 20 seeds for its larger-model mixture sweep. Synthetic seed counts and the existing 95% confidence intervals from 1,000 bootstrap samples are unchanged.

E6.justification: V4 updates Figure 7a and adds MMLU NLL distributions and a unimodal training-loss result, with mean 11.6245 and median 11.6179 in Figure 9. Its revised larger-model appendix reports bimodal accuracy and multimodal NLL, replacing v3's finding of a smoother, not clearly bimodal transition. These involve revised settings and newly reported results, not established same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: V4 Section 2.4 adds a mathematical continuity argument: token losses use fixed correct contexts, and the maximum of finitely many Lipschitz-continuous functions remains Lipschitz-continuous. The metric equations and Appendix B definitions are retained.

C1.justification: The distributional explanation of emergence and the inverse-scaling contribution remain. V4 explicitly frames discontinuities as probabilistic acquisition of discrete concepts and makes continuous-loss multimodality in both synthetic and natural-language tasks a separate main contribution.

C2.justification: V4 removes v3 Appendix E.2's qualification that larger-model bimodality may disappear, together with its latent-formatting-ability explanation. New Section 3.4 argues that continuous loss reveals failure clusters hidden by accuracy and attributes multimodality to emergent tasks rather than general training noise. These materially revise interpretation and applicability.

D1.justification: V4 adds a reproducibility statement promising code and data upon publication, without providing current access. It also explicitly documents correct-context token evaluation for the existing loss metric. Appendix A's hardware, runtime, and hyperparameter disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V4 adds Li et al. (2025), 'Can interpretation predict behavior on unseen data?', and expands its positioning against emergence and mirage/loss-to-downstream accounts. The earlier reference set and principal related-work themes remain; the citation-style conversion is presentational.

P1.justification: The title changes from 'Distributional Scaling of Emergent Capabilities' to 'Random Scaling of Emergent Capabilities'. V4 substantially rewrites the introduction, groups setup with each experimental domain, advances the continuous-metric discussion, and merges related work and conclusions into a Discussion section.

P2.justification: The LM visual presentation expands substantially through new loss and training-loss plots, paired accuracy/loss displays, and replacement of the larger-model violin plot with histogram/KDE panels. Figure 7a is redrawn, and the document adopts a different title/header layout. Existing synthetic and CSQA plots are retained, often relocated or renumbered.

improvement.justification: V4 strengthens the MMLU evidence through continuous-loss checks, a training-loss control, and larger reported seed populations, addressing alternative explanations left untested on LMs in v3. The gain is limited by the revised larger-model appendix: its changed mixture grid and bimodality conclusion are not reconciled with v3's earlier qualification. Overall, the added validation supports a limited improvement.
